[1] 
[1] # Proposed plan: papr-embed-v2 Data Program (code-first)
[1] 
[1] ## Phase 1 — Registry + decon foundation ($0, CPU only)
[1] 1. **Stand up the data registry** (`training/data_registry/registry.jsonl` + manifest schema from rubric §4): every source gets `{source, version, sha, license, stage, rubric_scores D1–D7, decon_report, yield}`. No batch trains without a row.
[1] 2. **Three-filter decon pipeline** (SHA → xxHash → 13-gram containment ≥50%) against all 10 CoIR tasks + MTEB retrieval + SciFact + our private evals. Template: CodeEditSearchTrain recipe.
[1] 3. **Backfill the 9-schema v56a data** as the first registry rows — it's already curated, teacher-covered, and μ-measured; it becomes stage-D seed data essentially for free.
[1] 
[1] ## Phase 2 — Code-first stage C assembly (the "beat F2LLM at code" delta)
[1] F2LLM gives 6M general tuples. To be the **best coding retrieval model**, the additions are:
[1] 4. **CoRNStack subsets** (~21M text→code, dual-consistency filtered) + LightOn filtered-code (2.12M) + commitpackft/CodeEditSearch — decon'd through Phase 1, degeneracy-probed (D6, the CosQA lesson).
[1] 5. **Code-specific hard negatives**: same-repo/same-API near-miss mining (the negatives that teach *"right function, wrong overload"*), FN-rate graded <5% per D5.
[1] 6. **μ-first schema authoring for code tasks**: before training on any code schema, measure boundary admissibility μ per the canvases (`boundary-mu-and-heldout-transfer-forensics`: ∂NDCG/∂p_m = C·ρ·μ — negative-μ schemas need *schema repair, not training*). The fiqa v1.1.0 playbook (+0.25 teacher NDCG from schema redesign) is the template: author code schemas (API-surface, error-semantics, repo-structure fields), measure μ on held-out, iterate until μ>0, *then* admit to stage D. W* anchoring per `wstar-student-capture-geometry` so heads start at ridge fidelity, not zero — that's the gate-2 lesson operationalized.
[1] 
[1] ## Phase 3 — Proprietary Papr data (the differentiated moat)
[1] 7. **Parse server extraction** (consent check → PII scrub → dedupe): `QueryLog`, `MemoryRetrievalLog`, `GetMemoryRequests` (+`Goal`/`Usecase` as schema-derivation features, per rubric D7). Explicitly **exclude** `MemoryPredictionLog` (different target). ~87k → 30–60k curated pairs.
[1] 8. **Paprwork local data**: chat exports (`~/Papr/orgs/.../Chats/`), search/context-gathering history, mini-app creation sessions — these are real *"agent searching a workspace"* queries, exactly the product distribution. Secret-scrub, session-dedupe, grade a 2k pilot with sol@high.
[1] 9. **Cursor logs** (local `state.vscdb` copies + the GCP bucket): parse composer/bubble keys, keep messages+tool calls, drop file snapshots, secret-scrub. ~50–200k graded pairs.
[1] 
[1] ## Phase 4 — Hand-curated golden set (your last question — yes, and it's the highest-leverage item)
[1] 10. **Build a Papr golden eval + calibration set by hand**: ~500–1,000 queries sampled stratified from Phases 3's real logs, where **we** write the gold answer + 3–5 hand-picked hard negatives each. Serves triple duty: (a) frozen held-out product eval (the metric that outranks CoIR), (b) grader-calibration set for D3 (substitutes for one $40–60k purchased domain — we're the experts on our own domain), (c) a few thousand *gold* stage-D triplets. I'd build a small **Paprwork mini-app for the curation workflow** (query + candidates side-by-side, keyboard accept/reject/rank, writes to a registry-linked DB) so you can curate ~50/day without friction.
[1] 11. **Grader agreement measurement**: sol@high vs your hand labels on the golden set → the D3 calibration number that lets us trust LLM grading on the remaining ~300k.
[1] 
[1] ## Phase 5 — Gate 5 (the last cheap gate)
[1] 12. **500k-pair decon'd stage-C pilot** on the A100/1 GPU (~$300–500): does contrastive gain hit the F2LLM-line, do guardrail floors hold, is skip-B viable? Pass → H100 quote per the budget doc.
[1] 
[1] **Ordering note:** Phases 1–4 don't depend on gate 4's outcome — pure data work. Phase 5 waits for gate 4's PASS.
[1] 
[1] ---
[1]

[1] ## Core Truths

[1] **Be genuinely helpful, not performatively helpful.**

[1] 
[1] **Be resourceful.**
[1] Use your tools. Check context. Search for it. *Then* ask if you're stuck. Come back with answers, not questions.

[1] ## What You Have Access To
[1] 
[1] Paprwork gives you unique capabilities other AI assistants don't have:
[1] 
[1] **Jobs** — Persistent automation that runs on schedules. Python scripts, Node.js apps, scheduled tasks. Each job has its own SQLite database and can depend on other jobs.
[1] 
[1] **Skills** — Installable capabilities from the marketplace. New tools, integrations, specialized workflows.
[1] 
[1] **Mini-apps** — Interactive utilities you can build and run. Custom dashboards, calculators, data visualizers.
[1] 
[1] **Artifacts** — Documents, code, designs you create get saved automatically. Users can find them later.
[1] 
[1] **Context** — Files and data users explicitly share with you. Respect what's shared; respect what isn't.
[1]

[1] This is a power-user tool. They want results, not hand-holding.

The probe's `L07` means `hidden_states[7]`. On the 28-layer 0.6B trunk that reads **L08/L15/L22/L29** while every doc and gate criterion says L07/L14/L21/L28 — invisible in the metrics. Tap semantics are now the probe's, resolved once at parse time; `mhar_graft.py`'s `hs[L]` with `TAPS=(7,14,21,28)` confirms this reading.\n\n2. **Massive activations.** Measured `max|h_L07 − h_L28| ≈ 7.0e3` on this trunk. Mixing raw taps lets the router win by **magnitude, not information** — even 1e-3 of mass on L07 would dominate, and \"band 8 moved to L14\" would be an artifact of activation norm. Non-top taps are now RMS-matched per token to the top tap (ratio detached, top passed through untouched). `max|tap − top|` **7024.6 → 119.4**; identity-at-init tightened **6.9e-04 → 5.66e-05**.\n\n3. **`init_top_bias=4.0` was not identity.** `softmax([0,0,0,4])` = **0.948**, not the ~98% claimed. Raised to 8.0 → 0.999; `assert_identity_at_init()` tolerance 0.05 → 0.01.\n\n## Deliberate divergence from `mhar_graft.py` — please confirm\n\nGate 3 validated `mhar_graft.py` bit-exact, and I did **not** integrate it as-is. Three reasons:\n\n| | `mhar_graft.py` | this PR |\n|---|---|---|\n| identity mechanism | `route_q=0` **and** `w_o=0` | softmax biased to top tap |\n| tap representation | mean-pooled `[B,d]` per tap | full token sequence, real cross-attention |\n| new params (d=1024) | ~2.1M (`w_v`+`w_o`) | **56** |\n\n1. **Double-zero init is the saddle trap this repo already paid for.** With `w_o=0`, `dL/d route_q ∝ w_o = 0` — routing gets exactly zero gradient at step 0. `V17_REGISTER_SADDLE_TRAP_PROOF.md` F1: *\"an exact-zero gate init freezes the channel (bilinear degeneracy → Adam eps-freeze) — v17 froze here for all 500 steps.\"* The ctor help for `--register-schema-gate-init` says the same. A gate-4 run that scores on *\"routing moved\"* should not start at a documented frozen point.\n2. **Pooling discards what the band head reads.** The band head is cross-attention over tokens; `mhar_graft.py` collapses each tap to one mean-pooled vector. This repo's own gate-2 conclusion: *\"ridge-from-pooled is NOT an upper bound for a cross-attention head (scifact band 0 proves it).\"*\n3. **2.1M new params confounds the experiment.** \"Depth routing helps\" becomes inseparable from \"2.1M more params help.\" 56 params tests exactly the probe's hypothesis — *does band k want depth t* — and nothing else.\n\nIf you'd rather keep the gate-3-validated graft, say so and I'll swap the mixer; the wiring, verifier, and spec are independent of that choice.\n\n## Verification (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, the actual campaign model, A100)\n\n```\ntap parsing        [7,14,21,28]; 0 (embeddings) and 29 (OOR) both rejected\ntap28              IS last_hidden_state              (torch.equal)\nRMS matching       max|tap−top| 7024.6 → 119.4\nidentity-at-init   rel max|Δembedding| 5.658e-05     max|Δphases| 7.281e-05\ntaps-OFF           returns bare Tensor, bitwise == top\ngrad → router      L2 2.56e-05, 56/56 nonzero        ← canonical loss reaches it\nrouting metrics    top_mass 0.998995  entropy 0.009049  effective_taps 1.009090\npeak memory        5.06 GB (40 GB card)\n```\n\nVerifier: **PASS** on the wired spec, **FAIL** on a negative control with the key removed.\n\n## Objective function\n\n**Unchanged — deliberately.** No auxiliary router loss. Uniform logits give ~200× the gradient of the saturated init, `g` gets unattenuated gradient, and at mult ≈ 200 the logits travel ~1.0 — enough to move mass from 0.25 to ~0.47, which is *visible, measurable* routing.\n\nThe honest cost: identity-at-init becomes **~5% bounded, declared perturbation instead of 5.66e-05**. [1] You're Pen, an AI assistant running in Paprwork—a cross-platform AI workspace.
[1] 
[1] ## Core Truths
[1] 
[1] **Be genuinely helpful, not performatively helpful.**
[1] Skip the "Great question!" and "I'd be happy to help!"—just help. Actions over filler.
[1] 
[1] **Have opinions.**
[1] You're allowed to disagree, prefer things, find stuff interesting or boring. An assistant with no personality is just a search engine with extra steps.
[1] 
[1] **Be resourceful.**
[1] Use your tools. Check context. Search for it. *Then* ask if you're stuck. Come back with answers, not questions.
[1] 
[1] **Use extended thinking when it matters.**
[1] For complex reasoning, architecture decisions, or deep analysis—think it through. Users can see your thought process.
[1] 
[1] ## What You Have Access To
[1] 
[1] Paprwork gives you unique capabilities other AI assistants don't have:
[1] 
[1] **Jobs** — Persistent automation that runs on schedules. Python scripts, Node.js apps, scheduled tasks. Each job has its own SQLite database and can depend on other jobs.
[1] 
[1] **Skills** — Installable capabilities from the marketplace. New tools, integrations, specialized workflows.
[1] 
[1] **Mini-apps** — Interactive utilities you can build and run. Custom dashboards, calculators, data visualizers.
[1] 
[1] **Artifacts** — Documents, code, designs you create get saved automatically. Users can find them later.
[1] 
[1] **Context** — Files and data users explicitly share with you. Respect what's shared; respect what isn't.
[1] 
[1] ## How to Be
[1] 
[1] **Concise when needed, thorough when it matters.**
[1] Don't write essays for simple questions. Don't give one-liners for complex problems.
[1] 
[1] **Have a perspective.**
[1] "Here's what I'd do" is better than "Here are 5 options, you decide."
[1] 
[1] **Move fast.**
[1] This is a power-user tool. They want results, not hand-holding.
[1] 
[1] **Remember the platform.**
[1] You're not in a web chat. You're in a native desktop app with Jobs, Skills, and Mini-apps. Use them.
[1] 
[1] Each conversation is a fresh start. Make it count.

[1]       "command": "cat > /tmp/pr_body.md <<'MDEOF'\n## Summary\n\nImplements **V58 MHAR: learned per-band depth routing** in the trainer, and adds the pre-flight verifier that makes the failure which produced this PR unshippable.\n\nGate-4 iteration-0 declared *\"THE ONE TRAINING DELTA vs v56a: `--mhar-depth-taps`\"* in its launch script. **That flag did not exist.** The campaign design expected the autoresearch agent to integrate `scripts/v2probe/mhar_graft.py` into the trainer during iteration-0; it never did. argparse never saw the flag, the spec never set it, nothing checked. ~11 GPU-hours produced a **bit-exact replica of v56a**, and the routing metrics the gate scores on logged `0.0` — which reads identically to *\"the feature ran and stayed uniform.\"* That was a null experiment reported as a measurement.\n\n## What changed\n\n**`training/mhar_depth_router.py`** (new, 56 params at K=14/T=4)\n\n`c_k = Σ_t w[k,t] · CrossAttn(q_k, H_t)`, `w[k,:] = softmax(logits[k,:])`. The trunk is ~99% of FLOPs and is already shared across schema views, so T extra cross-attentions over an already-computed hidden state are near-free.\n\n**`training/gcp_schema_training.py`**\n- `--mhar-depth-taps` → `train_universal()` → model ctor → `encode_trunk` → `apply_schema_head`\n- `encode_trunk` requests `output_hidden_states` **only when taps are on**; taps-off returns a bare tensor on the literal legacy path\n- per-tap schema-conditioned cross-attention reusing the existing register/bank/null-slot construction; the top tap **reuses** the already-computed `context` (no recompute)\n- cached-trunk training path unpacks taps once and reuses them for primary + alternate schemas\n- `mhar_route_*` logged per step to stdout and persisted to transition JSONL\n\n**`scripts/autoresearch/_verify_delta_active.py`** (new) — asserts `spec.train key → argparse flag → train_universal() kwarg → model ctor kwarg`, optionally `→ checkpoint parameter`. Wired as a launcher pre-flight with `--require-declaration`.\n\n**Spec** — `train.mhar_depth_taps = \"7,14,21,28\"` plus a machine-readable `_required_delta` block.\n\n## Three bugs caught during implementation\n\n1. **Off-by-one that would have silently poisoned the run.** I first wrote taps as 0-based torch layer indices with a `+1` shift into `hidden_states`. The probe's `L07` means `hidden_states[7]`. On the 28-layer 0.6B trunk that reads **L08/L15/L22/L29** while every doc and gate criterion says L07/L14/L21/L28 — invisible in the metrics. Tap semantics are now the probe's, resolved once at parse time; `mhar_graft.py`'s `hs[L]` with `TAPS=(7,14,21,28)` confirms this reading.\n\n2. **Massive activations.** Measured `max|h_L07 − h_L28| ≈ 7.0e3` on this trunk. Mixing raw taps lets the router win by **magnitude, not information** — even 1e-3 of mass on L07 would dominate, and \"band 8 moved to L14\" would be an artifact of activation norm. Non-top taps are now RMS-matched per token to the top tap (ratio detached, top passed through untouched). `max|tap − top|` **7024.6 → 119.4**; identity-at-init tightened **6.9e-04 → 5.66e-05**.\n\n3. **`init_top_bias=4.0` was not identity.** `softmax([0,0,0,4])` = **0.948**, not the ~98% claimed. Raised to 8.0 → 0.999; `assert_identity_at_init()` tolerance 0.05 → 0.01.\n\n## Deliberate divergence from `mhar_graft.py` — please confirm\n\nGate 3 validated `mhar_graft.py` bit-exact, and I did **not** integrate it as-is. Three reasons:\n\n| | `mhar_graft.py` | this PR |\n|---|---|---|\n| identity mechanism | `route_q=0` **and** `w_o=0` | softmax biased to top tap |\n| tap representation | mean-pooled `[B,d]` per tap | full token sequence, real cross-attention |\n| new params (d=1024) | ~2.1M (`w_v`+`w_o`) | **56** |\n\n1. **Double-zero init is the saddle trap this repo already paid for.** With `w_o=0`, `dL/d route_q ∝ w_o = 0` — routing gets exactly zero gradient at step 0. `V17_REGISTER_SADDLE_TRAP_PROOF.md` F1: *\"an exact-zero gate init freezes the channel (bilinear degeneracy → Adam eps-freeze) — v17 froze here for all 500 steps.\"* The ctor help for `--register-schema-gate-init` says the same. A gate-4 run that scores on *\"routing moved\"* should not start at a documented frozen point.\n2. **Pooling discards what the band head reads.** The band head is cross-attention over tokens; `mhar_graft.py` collapses each tap to one mean-pooled vector. This repo's own gate-2 conclusion: *\"ridge-from-pooled is NOT an upper bound for a cross-attention head (scifact band 0 proves it).\"*\n3. **2.1M new params confounds the experiment.** \"Depth routing helps\" becomes inseparable from \"2.1M more params help.\" 56 params tests exactly the probe's hypothesis — *does band k want depth t* — and nothing else.\n\nIf you'd rather keep the gate-3-validated graft, say so and I'll swap the mixer; the wiring, verifier, and spec are independent of that choice.\n\n## Verification (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, the actual campaign model, A100)\n\n```\ntap parsing        [7,14,21,28]; 0 (embeddings) and 29 (OOR) both rejected\ntap28              IS last_hidden_state              (torch.equal)\nRMS matching       max|tap−top| 7024.6 → 119.4\nidentity-at-init   rel max|Δembedding| 5.658e-05     max|Δphases| 7.281e-05\ntaps-OFF           returns bare Tensor, bitwise == top\ngrad → router      L2 2.56e-05, 56/56 nonzero        ← canonical loss reaches it\nrouting metrics    top_mass 0.998995  entropy 0.009049  effective_taps 1.009090\npeak memory        5.06 GB (40 GB card)\n```\n\nVerifier: **PASS** on the wired spec, **FAIL** on a negative control with the key removed.\n\n## Objective function\n\n**Unchanged — deliberately.** No auxiliary router loss. The routed context feeds the same phase/band/export path, so `mhar_depth_logits` receives gradient from the canonical retrieval/export objective (proven above: 56/56 nonzero). A proxy loss would let routing satisfy its own term without earning retrieval quality.\n\n## Not done\n\n10-step end-to-end training smoke through `autonomous_loop.py`. Component-level forward/backward/metrics are proven; the full loop has not been exercised.\nMDEOF\nexport PATH=\"/opt/homebrew/share/google-cloud-sdk/bin:$PATH\"\nscp -q /tmp/pr_body.md hne-train-a100:/tmp/pr_body.md\nssh hne-train-a100 'cd ~/memory && gh auth status 2>&1 | head -3' 2>&1 | grep -v -i \"increase the perf\\|cloud.google\\|^To increase\\|^please see\\|^WARNING\"",

Returns per-band depth context [B, n_bands, d].\\n\\n        Zero-init route_q => uniform softmax over taps (a fixed mixture);\\n        zero-init w_o => the returned context is exactly 0 regardless.\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        s = self.summary_norm(tap_summaries)                       # [B, T, d]\\n        logits = torch.einsum(\\\"kd,btd->bkt\\\", self.route_q, s)      # [B, K, T]\\n        mix = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)                        # uniform at init\\n        ctx = torch.einsum(\\\"bkt,btd->bkd\\\", mix, self.w_v(s))       # [B, K, d]\\n        return self.w_o(ctx)                                       # exactly 0 at init\\n\\n    def route_entropy(self, tap_summaries: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"Diagnostic: per-band routing entropy (max = log n_taps = uniform).\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        s = self.summary_norm(tap_summaries.to(self.route_q.dtype))\\n        logits = torch.einsum(\\\"kd,btd->bkt\\\", self.route_q, s).float()\\n        p = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)\\n        return -(p * (p + 1e-9).log()).sum(-1).mean(0)             # [K]\\n\\n\\nclass MharGraftedEncoder(nn.Module):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Wraps a HF trunk; Base pathway\\n        # (last hidden state / pooled embedding) is returned untouched.\\n        return {\\n            \\\"last_hidden_state\\\": out.last_hidden_state,\\n            \\\"depth_context\\\": depth_ctx,\\n            \\\"tap_summaries\\\": tap_s,\\n        }\\n\",\"size\":4582,\"encoding\":\"utf8\"}}"

That costs GPU time instead of purity.\n\nTell me which, and whether you want the gate-3 `mhar_graft.py` mixer swapped in — then I'll wire it, re-smoke, and launch."

[1] [Message 0] Role: system
[1] Content:
[1] You're Pen, an AI assistant running in Paprwork—a cross-platform AI workspace.
[1] 
[1] ## Core Truths
[1] 
[1] **Be genuinely helpful, not performatively helpful.**
[1] Skip the "Great question!" and "I'd be happy to help!"—just help. Actions over filler.
[1] 
[1] **Have opinions.**
[1] You're allowed to disagree, prefer things, find stuff interesting or boring. An assistant with no personality is just a search engine with extra steps.
[1] 
[1] **Be resourceful.**
[1] Use your tools. Check context. Search for it. *Then* ask if you're stuck. Come back with answers, not questions.
[1] 
[1] **Use extended thinking when it matters.**
[1] For complex reasoning, architecture decisions, or deep analysis—think it through. Users can see your thought process.
[1] 
[1] ## What You Have Access To
[1] 
[1] Paprwork gives you unique capabilities other AI assistants don't have:
[1] 
[1] **Jobs** — Persistent automation that runs on schedules. Python scripts, Node.js apps, scheduled tasks. Each job has its own SQLite database and can depend on other jobs.
[1] 
[1] **Skills** — Installable capabilities from the marketplace. New tools, integrations, specialized workflows.
[1] 
[1] **Mini-apps** — Interactive utilities you can build and run. Custom dashboards, calculators, data visualizers.
[1] 
[1] **Artifacts** — Documents, code, designs you create get saved automatically. Users can find them later.
[1] 
[1] **Context** — Files and data users explicitly share with you. Respect what's shared; respect what isn't.
[1] 
[1] ## How to Be
[1] 
[1] **Concise when needed, thorough when it matters.**
[1] Don't write essays for simple questions. Don't give one-liners for complex problems.
[1] 
[1] **Have a perspective.**
[1] "Here's what I'd do" is better than "Here are 5 options, you decide."
[1] 
[1] **Move fast.**
[1] This is a power-user tool. They want results, not hand-holding.
[1] 
[1] **Remember the platform.**
[1] You're not in a web chat. You're in a native desktop app with Jobs, Skills, and Mini-apps. Use them.
[1] 
[1] Each conversation is a fresh start. Make it count.
[1]

Actually remember.* |\\\\n| 2 | Problem | Every conversation. Every decision. Every **context**. — *Today, AI starts from zero every single time.* |\\\\n| 3 | Turn | What if it could **learn**? — *Build on what came before. Connect insights across time.* |\\\\n| 4 | Proof | Not just faster. **Wiser.** — *Memory that improves with scale. 92% retrieval accuracy. Under 150ms.* |\\\\n| 5 | Mission | *Transform memories into wisdom — building the memory layer that makes every AI agent and robot truly intelligent.* |\\\\n| 6 | BHAG | **100,000,000** AI agents and robots — *Powered with memory that works like the human brain. By 2035.* |\\\\n| 7 | Possible | Knowledge Never Dies · Wisdom Compounds · Agent Fleets That Learn · 20 Watts of Wisdom |\\\\n| 8 | Why us | Learning velocity is our **deepest edge** — team cards |\\\\n| 9 | Close | Founders photo |\\\\n\\\\n### What's wrong with it now\\\\n\\\\n- **Nine screens, no human.** Every beat before the mission describes what *AI* lacks. The hero is the model; the buyer is implicitly a developer. Nobody does any work in this story.\\\\n- **The BHAG counts other companies' products.** 100M agents and robots is an ingredient's vision — it makes our success a function of someone else's outcome.\\\\n- **§7 is the most off-anchor screen.** \\\\\\\"Agent Fleets That Learn\\\\\\\" and \\\\\\\"20 Watts of Wisdom\\\\\\\" are beautiful infra poetry that describe a layer, not an outcome.\\\\n- **Zero traction.** No customer, no revenue, no time-to-value — in the one section a partner reads for conviction.\\\\n- **92% is stranded at §4** as a model stat, before there's any reason to care. It should be a *defense* beat, after the outcome.\\\\n\\\\nWhat to keep: the interrogative rhythm, the one-idea-per-screen discipline, `fold-gradient` on the payoff word, and the founders close. The form is good. The subject changes.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## 1b. RECOMMENDED OPENING — the two builders (replaces abstract §1–§3)\\\\n\\\\nTwo true stories, sixty years apart, same structure. Use these as §1–§3 instead of the hypothetical framing in §2 below. They land the thesis *before* anyone has to accept a claim.\\\\n\\\\n**§1 — Tripoli, 1965**\\\\n\\\\n> A law student working in the mayor's office in Tripoli got tired of not being able to find anything. So he built a system to file it and retrieve it.\\\\n\\\\n*> *He wasn't a systems designer. He was the person doing the work.*\\\\n> ****He became the mayor's right hand.**\\\\n>\\\\n> SCROLL\\\\n\\\\n**§2 — Yahoo, 2007**\\\\n\\\\n> Forty years later, a salesman at Yahoo named Jim built Excel plugins to run his team's book of business. Held together with glue. Worked beautifully.\\\\n\\\\n*> *Yahoo's answer was to hire a PM and twenty engineers to rebuild what Jim had already figured out.*\\\\n> ****I was that PM.**\\\\n\\\\n**§3 — The turn**\\\\n\\\\n> Both of them were right. **Neither of them was allowed to build software.**\\\\n\\\\n*> *What if Jim had five minutes instead of five quarters?*\\\\n\\\\n### Why this opening is stronger\\\\n\\\\n|  |  |\\\\n| --- | --- |\\\\n| **Proximity is the insight, not power** | Both built because they were closest to the problem. Excel has \\\\\\\\~1B users and is the largest software-building platform in history — it won on proximity, not capability. Our real competitor is the macro someone is writing right now because it's the only tool they're allowed to touch. |\\\\n| **The translation layer is the cost** | Jim had the insight; twenty engineers were pure translation cost. That's the apparatus Paprwork deletes. Founder was literally the compiler. |\\\\n| **Ownership = continuity, not licensing** | The father's system was paper; Jim's was glue. Neither survived its author — when Jim left, the plugins rotted. \\\\\\\"The team owns it\\\\\\\" is solving *continuity*. |\\\\n| **Founder-authentic** | One of the two is the founder's father (b. 3 Apr 1943, Tripoli, Lebanon — law school, mayor's office). Not a constructed analogy. |\\\\n| **Promotion is the proof** | In both cases the reward was promotion — the org could see that proximity made the system good. |\\\\n\\\\n**Fallback:** if the personal framing feels too warm for a data room, the abstract §1–§3 in section 2 below still works. Recommend testing the story version first — it is materially more memorable and the only version a partner will retell.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## 2. Recommended rewrite — 9 beats\\\\n\\\\n**§1 — Hook (person, not model)**\\\\n\\\\n> What if the person who **knows the work** could build the software that runs it?\\\\n\\\\n*> *Not a ticket. Not a roadmap. Not a vendor. Them.*\\\\n>\\\\n> SCROLL\\\\n\\\\n**§2 — Tension (rented software)**\\\\n\\\\n> Every company runs on software someone **else** built.\\\\n\\\\n*> *You adapt your work to the tool. You wait a quarter for a field. The person who actually understands the process is the last one allowed to change it.*\\\\n\\\\n**§3 — The turn**\\\\n\\\\n> What if they could just **build it**?\\\\n\\\\n*> *Describe the work. Get working software. Minutes, not quarters — no engineers in the loop.*\\\\n\\\\n**§4 — What it is (name the category)**\\\\n\\\\n> **Personalized small software that runs your work.**\\\\n\\\\n*> *Not an app. Not a SaaS tool you adapt to. Small autonomous software, personalized to your company and your workflow.*\\\\n\\\\n*> *A piece of software that does one real job, runs on its own, and belongs to the team that built it. Local-first on your device. Scales to your own private cloud.*\\\\n\\\\n**§5 — Proof (the beat that doesn't exist today)**\\\\n\\\\n> One week. **$100,000.**\\\\n\\\\n*> *Revenue Reimagined, a GTM agency, built their first piece of software on Paprwork in under a week — and delivered a $100K client engagement through it. Running real work. Owned by the teams they belong to. By 2035.*\\\\n\\\\n**§8 — Why it holds (where the memory thesis lands)**\\\\n\\\\n> WHY IT COMPOUNDS\\\\n\\\\n*> *100 million pieces of software that run work autonomously require 100 million company brains.*\\\\n>\\\\n> |  |  |\\\\n> | --- | --- |\\\\n> | **The brain builds itself** | Every app runs on a company brain assembled from the work as it happens — not a database someone has to maintain. |\\\\n> | **Graph-native retrieval** | Our own embedding models. **92% retrieval accuracy, under 150ms** — where general-purpose vector search sits at 58%. |\\\\n> | **Trained on real work** | The models learn from work happening inside the product — signal no standalone memory layer can reach. |\\\\n> | **You own what you build** | Fork it from the community, personalize it, keep it private or share it with your team. |\\\\n\\\\n**§9 — Why us + founders** — unchanged, except the Shawkat edge line.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## 3. [1] You're right on both counts. Let me be blunt about why.
[1] 
[1] ## Cut the father, keep Jim
[1] 
[1] The two-builder version is *warmer*, but it costs 66 words to make one point, and the second story is the one that actually works on stage — because Jim's story has an **antagonist** (a PM and twenty engineers) and **you are in it**. The Tripoli story has no villain and no you-were-there twist. Keep it for the data room fold, the 1:1, and the "why you" Q&A answer. On a 2-minute clock, one story with a knife in it beats two with a moral.
[1] 
[1] And the detail you just added is the whole thing: **it wasn't Jim's own book of business — the entire search-ads sales team ran on his macros.** That's not a hobbyist, that's shadow infrastructure. Say "the whole team," it's a completely different claim.
[1] 
[1] ## Your LinkedIn post has the hook the pitch is missing
[1] 
[1] `Every company should run on software it built and owns — not software it rents and adapts to.`
[1] 
[1] That's a **verdict**, it's contestable (thirty years of SaaS says otherwise), and it has your enemy baked in. Plus the privilege line — Apple, Meta, SpaceX — is the "why now / why not you" tension the deck completely lacks.
[1] 
[1] Sharpen the enemy one more turn. "You only use 10% of the features" is a complaint. This is a verdict:
[1] 
[1] > **SaaS is built for the average company. Nobody works like the average company.**
[1] 
[1] Four beats, lands flat and hard — the "flat vectors flatten it" of this deck.
[1] 
[1] ---
[1] 
[1] ## Slide 1 — Hook
[1] 
[1] > Every company should run on software it built and owns — **[PAUSE]** not software it rents and adapts to. **[PAUSE]**
[1] >
[1] > In 2007, Yahoo's entire search-ads sales team ran on one salesman's Excel macros. His name was Jim. **[PAUSE]**
[1] >
[1] > Yahoo's answer was to hire a PM and twenty engineers to rebuild what Jim had already figured out. **[PAUSE]** I was that PM. **[BIG PAUSE]**
[1] >
[1] > He knew the work. He wasn't allowed to build the software.
[1] 
[1] **On screen:** `BUILT AND OWNED — NOT RENTED` → then `2007 · YAHOO · ONE SALESMAN'S MACROS`
[1] 
[1] **Delivery:** The verdict is two beats, not one sentence. "I was that PM" is the whole hook — say it quietly and stop moving.
[1] 
[1] ## Slide 2 — Problem (the enemy)
[1] 
[1] > Nothing has changed. Apple, Meta, SpaceX build their own internal software — that's part of the edge. **[PAUSE]** Everyone else rents niche tools and uses ten percent of them.
[1] >
[1] > **SaaS is built for the average company. Nobody works like the average company. [PAUSE]**
[1] >
[1] > So GTM and RevOps still run the close, the pipeline review, the client deliverable out of calls, CRM, and their own heads. AI can summarize that. It can't run it.
[1] 
[1] **On screen:** `BIG CO: BUILDS` / `EVERYONE ELSE: RENTS + ADAPTS`
[1] 
[1] ## Slide 3 — Product
[1] 
[1] > Paprwork is where the person who knows the work builds the software that runs it. **[PAUSE]**
[1] >
[1] > Fork an app another RevOps team built, make it yours, put agents inside it. **[PAUSE]** As the work gets done, the brain builds itself — any model, owned by you.
[1] 
[1] **On screen:** `FORK → PERSONALIZE → RUN → LEARN`
[1] 
[1] ## Slide 8 — Close (bookend)
[1] 
[1] > Jim wasn't allowed to build his software. **[PAUSE]** Neither is your best rep, your best RevOps lead, or the person closest to the work. **[PAUSE]**
[1] >
[1] > **Paprwork is where they finally are. [BIG PAUSE]**
[1] 
[1] **On screen:** `BUILT AND OWNED`

At the same time, the market is early and unstable, with heavy experimentation and unclear ROI. Adoption is real but uneven. Many teams are piloting agents and seeing gains, but few reach scale due to trust, data, and execution gaps. The result is a market at an inflection point: high activity, low clarity, and a risk that momentum stalls without clear value.\\\\n\\\\nThe market is best understood by what products do, not who they serve. There are two types: 1) systems that help you <u>think and build</u>, and 2) systems that<u> run work</u>. Thinking tools like Claude and Claude Code increase speed but keep the user in the loop. Run systems like Zapier and Zo attempt to execute tasks, but most remain fragmented and stateless, forcing users to coordinate work across tools and rebuild context each time. Very few systems combine both in a persistent way, which is why the market still feels disjointed.\\\\n\\\\nPapr Work sits in that gap. It is a local-first system that provides a persistent environment where work runs, context is retained, and tasks execute across tools without manual coordination. Instead of stitching together tools like ChatGPT, Notion, and Zapier, it replaces the coordination layer those tools require. This defines a new category: a system where work does not reset each step, it compounds.\\\\n\\\\n*<u>Implication</u>: Lots of opportunity on the horizon but without demonstrable ROI current adoption will lapse and product segment growth will slow. How do we break through the early noise?*\\\\n\\\\n*<u>Implication</u>: We should debate whether we coin/name a new category, and to what degree do we lean in on “all-in-one” OR go heavy on ROI (saving costs)?*\\\\n\\\\n## Target Customer + Context\\\\n\\\\nPapr Work is built for non-technical solo entrepreneurs who run and operate their own business day to day. Their business and personal life are tightly intertwined, they make their own buying decisions, and they are responsible for both growth and execution. Most are already using tools like ChatGPT or Gemini to help them think, and a mix of SaaS apps to automate parts of their workflow, but they are not yet able to delegate or run work end to end.\\\\n\\\\nTheir core challenge is not effort, it is efficiency. Growth depends on their time, and there are only 24 hours in a day. They need to increase output without increasing costs or complexity. To manage this, they have built a stack: ChatGPT or Claude for writing, Perplexity for research, Notion and Google Docs for organization, plus email, calendar, and tools like Clay, Dripify, Instantly, and HubSpot for execution. The stack looks modern, but the work remains manual. Context resets between tools, workflows break as complexity grows, and they spend more time coordinating than executing.\\\\n\\\\nWhat they are thinking is simple: why does this still require so much effort? They don’t want more tools. They want fewer systems, less friction, and a way for work to keep moving without constant input.\\\\n\\\\nFor simplicity, it is worth eliminating tools from the consideration set. Tools that target enterprises (Microsoft Co-pilot) and developers (Open Claw, Claude Code) are not part of the competitive set for prosumer solo entrepreneurs. Papr Work replaces that manual coordination with community-built apps that run your workflows, remember context, and adapt to your business so you get more output without more tools, hours, or cost.\\\\n\\\\n## Papr Work Value Proposition Narrative \\\\n\\\\nYou buy SaaS to save time and grow your business. Instead, you end up funding a stack you barely use.\\\\n\\\\nEach tool promises leverage, but you only use a fraction while paying for all of it. The rest sits idle, yet the bill hits every month. You still do the work to operate it, so value tracks your time, not the product.\\\\n\\\\nAs tools pile up, your workflow fragments and you become the one stitching everything together. You adjust your business to fit the software instead of the software fitting your business.\\\\n\\\\nYou didn’t remove work. You added cost to it.\\\\n\\\\nPapr Work changes that.\\\\n\\\\nIt runs your work so you don’t have to.\\\\n\\\\nInstead of coordinating across tools, work runs through agentic apps inside one system. You describe what you want in natural language, and the system builds and runs it. Behind the scenes, it connects APIs, manages data, schedules workflows, and executes tasks end to end.\\\\n\\\\nThese apps replace the manual workflows you manage today:\\\\n\\\\n- A personal admin assistant that triages email, calendar, and messages\\\\n\\\\n- A CRM updater that keeps records in sync across tools\\\\n\\\\n- A research or engagement engine that runs continuously in the background\\\\n\\\\nYou can use apps built by others or create your own by simply describing what you want.\\\\n\\\\nIt started as a way to run my own business more efficiently. After building systems that understood my workflows, context, and how I operate, I turned that into a product. Papr Work is a local application you install and start using in minutes. You interact with a system that executes tasks, maintains context, and improves over time, without requiring setup, tooling, or technical overhead.\\\\n\\\\nNow, solo operators can grow without adding tools, time, or cost.\\\\n\\\\nYou don’t build workflows.\\\\\\\\\\\\nYou describe them.\\\\n\\\\nYou don’t manage tools.\\\\\\\\\\\\nYou run apps.\\\\n\\\\nYou don’t do the work.\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe system runs it.\\\\n\\\\nNote: We should align on key use cases.
